output.title: When date ambiguity stops working
output.body:
If you run a 1-10-person business and dates keep causing delays, the question is not whether AI can read a date. It is whether date ambiguity has become a recurring workflow problem.

You see it in the same places again and again: a missing timezone, a mixed date format, a deadline that appears differently in email, a form, and a spreadsheet. One person stops work to check what is meant. That is not a language problem; it is a workflow control problem.

For a small business, the decision is usually one of three: keep doing manual checks, hire someone to watch the queue, or automate one narrow step that standardises dates at the point of entry and flags anything unclear before it spreads. That is a fit check, not a promise. If your dates come from one place and one format, the issue may be too small to touch. If they come from several digital tools, the mess will keep inventing itself. Very considerate, in a hostile way.

A practical next step is simple: watch one recurring workflow for a week and note every time date ambiguity forces a pause, a clarification, or a correction. Count the interruptions, not the feelings. If the same confusion keeps showing up, you have a repeatable control problem. Human approval still stays in charge, especially anywhere money or other high-risk decisions are involved.
